extracted.intended_audience: students, writers, and scholars interested in comedy theory and dark/black humor
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for creating or evaluating dark/black humor works that treat taboo or painful subjects by juxtaposing pain and amusement to provoke discomfort, thought, and laughter. Emphasizes topic choice, treatment (juxtaposition/tonal control), audience distance, cognitive payoff, and ethical/earned handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic: taboo or painful
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the topic taboo or painful?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical topics covered include death, disease; deformity, handicap; warfare, atrocities; mental illness; despair, suicide. The defining feature of black humor is that it 'makes light of subject matter generally considered taboo — particularly subjects normally considered serious or painful — to provoke discomfort, serious thought, and amusement.' Use these subject areas as canonical source material but be mindful of context and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment: juxtaposition with calm/whimsy
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the treatment juxtaposed with calm/whimsy?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Academic characterization: black humor 'juxtaposes pain and joy, whimsical facts and unevenly calm reactions, cruelty and tenderness.' Effective black comedy pairs grotesque or morbid elements with whimsical or oddly calm presentation to highlight absurdity, insensitivity, paradox, and cruelty. Avoid purely abrasive or uniformly frantic tones; the contrast between tone and subject is a key quality signal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive payoff: offers insight, not mere shock
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it offer cognitive insight, not just shock?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Black humor should do more than provoke a startled reaction — it should yield cognitive insight, reveal absurdities, or prompt serious thought alongside amusement. Anti-pattern: content that is merely transgressive or shocking without deeper observation, commentary, or ironic distance (e.g., 'sick jokes' that rely only on shock value). The humor should illuminate or reframe the subject, not exploit it gratuitously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience psychological distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the audience have psychological distance from the subject?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective black humor typically requires that the audience have sufficient psychological distance from the topic so they can process the juxtaposition and perceive the intended insight. If the audience is directly and immediately harmed or identified with the subject, the same material may feel cruel or offensive rather than comic. Consider target audience proximity when evaluating appropriateness and likely reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earnedness vs. gratuitousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it feel earned, not gratuitous?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material should feel justified by context, character, or argument; the transgression must serve an expressive purpose. Anti-patterns include gratuitous cruelty or transgression that appears to exist only to offend. 'Gallows humor' and 'tragicomedy' often feel earned because they arise from characters' real situations; 'sick jokes' can feel unearned when they lack grounding or purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions / intended purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: What function does the black humor serve (coping, social, political)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Black humor can serve coping functions (allowing individuals to process difficult situations, aiding long-term stress reduction, helping acceptance of anxiety-inducing events) and social/political functions (strengthening morale of the oppressed, undermining morale of oppressors). When producing or evaluating work, consider which of these functions it is meant to perform and whether it succeeds at that aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive demands / audience traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the material match the cognitive and personality traits required to process it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research indicates black-humor processing requires high verbal intelligence, mood stability, and low aggressiveness; appreciators often are less aggressive and more verbally able. When crafting or evaluating black humor, account for these processing demands — complex juxtaposition and ambivalent tones may fail with audiences lacking the required cognitive or emotional resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtype suitability (gallows, sick joke, tragicomedy, cringe)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the chosen subtype of black humor appropriate and handled correctly?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common subtypes: 'gallows humor' (about one's own dire fate), 'sick joke' (extremely transgressive content), 'tragicomedy' (balanced pain and laughter), and 'cringe comedy' (derived from characters' pain). Each subtype has different tonal and ethical expectations: e.g., gallows humor often reads as coping and can be more acceptable to sufferers, while sick jokes risk appearing gratuitous. Choose and execute subtype with attention to earnedness and audience distance.
